claim: Social interactions and the overall psychosocial environment have a demonstrated impact on health, particularly for people living in disadvantaged urban areas.
source: Social interactions and the overall psychosocial environment have a demonstrated impact on health, particularly for people living in disadvantaged urban areas.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader literature and the study's findings.

claim: Using RNA-sequencing and a new machine learning approach, the study identified transcriptional signatures of 19 variables including psychosocial factors, blood cell composition, and asthma symptoms.
source: Using RNA-sequencing and a new machine learning approach, we identified transcriptional signatures of 19 variables including psychosocial factors, blood cell composition, and asthma symptoms.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the methods and results sections describing the machine learning approach and the identification of transcriptional signatures.

claim: 169 genes associated with asthma or allergic disease are regulated by psychosocial factors.
source: Importantly, we found 169 genes associated with asthma or allergic disease that are regulated by psychosocial factors and 344 significant gene-environment interactions for gene expression levels.
evidence: This is a specific finding reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: 344 significant gene-environment interactions for gene expression levels were identified.
source: Importantly, we found 169 genes associated with asthma or allergic disease that are regulated by psychosocial factors and 344 significant gene-environment interactions for gene expression levels.
evidence: This is a specific finding reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: Immune gene expression mediates the link between negative psychosocial experiences and asthma risk.
source: These results demonstrate that immune gene expression mediates the link between negative psychosocial experiences and asthma risk.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the integration of TWAS analysis and GxE mapping results.

claim: Psychosocial experiences have long been recognized to affect human health (Miller et al., 2009).
source: Psychosocial experiences have long been recognized to affect human health (Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2009.

claim: Intrapersonal processes (e.g., emotionality) are associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma.
source: Intrapersonal processes (e.g., emotionality [Pressman et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2004], interpersonal social relationships [Repetti et al., 2002; Robles et al., 2014]) and broader structural environments (e.g., neighborhood quality and socioeconomic status [SES]; Gallo and Matthews, 2003) are all associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma (Harrison, 1998), cancer (Meyer and Mark, 1995), cardiovascular disease (Everson-Rose and Lewis, 2005), as well as mortality rates (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010; Chida and Steptoe, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Pressman et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2004; and Harrison, 1998.

claim: Interpersonal social relationships are associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma.
source: Intrapersonal processes (e.g., emotionality [Pressman et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2004], interpersonal social relationships [Repetti et al., 2002; Robles et al., 2014]) and broader structural environments (e.g., neighborhood quality and socioeconomic status [SES]; Gallo and Matthews, 2003) are all associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma (Harrison, 1998), cancer (Meyer and Mark, 1995), cardiovascular disease (Everson-Rose and Lewis, 2005), as well as mortality rates (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010; Chida and Steptoe, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Repetti et al., 2002; Robles et al., 2014; and Harrison, 1998.

claim: Broader structural environments (e.g., neighborhood quality and socioeconomic status) are associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma.
source: Intrapersonal processes (e.g., emotionality [Pressman et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2004], interpersonal social relationships [Repetti et al., 2002; Robles et al., 2014]) and broader structural environments (e.g., neighborhood quality and socioeconomic status [SES]; Gallo and Matthews, 2003) are all associated with the morbidity and severity of diseases such as asthma (Harrison, 1998), cancer (Meyer and Mark, 1995), cardiovascular disease (Everson-Rose and Lewis, 2005), as well as mortality rates (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010; Chida and Steptoe, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Gallo and Matthews, 2003; and Harrison, 1998.

claim: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the respiratory tract that disproportionately affects children (Moorman et al., 2012).
source: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the respiratory tract that disproportionately affects children (Moorman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moorman et al., 2012.

claim: Asthma is one of the costliest pediatric health conditions (Weiss et al., 2000).
source: It is one of the costliest pediatric health conditions (Weiss et al., 2000) and a leading cause of school absenteeism (Akinbami and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Center for Health Statistics, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2000.

claim: Asthma is a leading cause of school absenteeism (Akinbami and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Center for Health Statistics, 2006).
source: It is one of the costliest pediatric health conditions (Weiss et al., 2000) and a leading cause of school absenteeism (Akinbami and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Center for Health Statistics, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Akinbami and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Center for Health Statistics, 2006.

claim: Financially struggling cities, such as Detroit, are at an especially high risk for asthma morbidity and mortality (Sullivan et al., 2002).
source: Financially struggling cities, such as Detroit, are at an especially high risk for asthma morbidity and mortality (Sullivan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sullivan et al., 2002.

claim: Environmental and genetic factors lead to the development of asthma and affect the health of children with asthma (von Mutius, 2000; von Mutius, 2009; Umetsu et al., 2002).
source: While environmental and genetic factors lead to the development of asthma and affect the health of children with asthma (von Mutius, 2000; von Mutius, 2009; Umetsu et al., 2002), psychosocial stress is a critical factor contributing to asthma severity (Wright et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2005; Shankardass et al., 2009; Chen and Miller, 2007; Sandberg et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including von Mutius, 2000; von Mutius, 2009; Umetsu et al., 2002.

claim: Psychosocial stress is a critical factor contributing to asthma severity (Wright et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2005; Shankardass et al., 2009; Chen and Miller, 2007; Sandberg et al., 2000).
source: While environmental and genetic factors lead to the development of asthma and affect the health of children with asthma (von Mutius, 2000; von Mutius, 2009; Umetsu et al., 2002), psychosocial stress is a critical factor contributing to asthma severity (Wright et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2005; Shankardass et al., 2009; Chen and Miller, 2007; Sandberg et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Wright et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2005; Shankardass et al., 2009; Chen and Miller, 2007; Sandberg et al., 2000.

claim: Understanding the biological pathways underlying associations between psychosocial experiences and health is crucial to strengthen the causal claims linking psychosocial experiences and health.
source: Understanding the biological pathways underlying these associations is crucial to strengthen the causal claims linking psychosocial experiences and health.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's rationale and motivation.

claim: The growing field of social genomics investigates how various dimensions of a person's social and psychological environment influence gene expression (Cole, 2014; Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2009; Toyokawa et al., 2012; Galea et al., 2011).
source: The growing field of social genomics investigates how various dimensions of a person's social and psychological environment influence gene expression (Cole, 2014; Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2009; Toyokawa et al., 2012; Galea et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Cole, 2014; Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2009; Toyokawa et al., 2012; Galea et al., 2011.

claim: There is ample evidence for links between gene expression in blood and three major categories of psychosocial experiences: SES (Chen et al., 2009), social relationships (Robles et al., 2018; Stanton et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2013), and emotionality (Farrell et al., 2018; Segman et al., 2010).
source: There is ample evidence for links between gene expression in blood and three major categories of psychosocial experiences: SES (Chen et al., 2009), social relationships (Robles et al., 2018; Stanton et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2013), and emotionality (Farrell et al., 2018; Segman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations for each category of psychosocial experiences.

claim: Previous studies identified a pattern of differentially expressed genes referred to as the conserved transcriptional response to adversity (CTRA) (Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2014; Cole, 2009).
source: Beyond single-gene analyses, previous studies in this area (Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2014; Cole, 2009) identified a pattern of differentially expressed genes referred to as the conserved transcriptional response to adversity (CTRA).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Slavich and Cole, 2013; Cole, 2014; Cole, 2009.

claim: The CTRA is characterized by increased expression of genes involved in inflammation and decreased expression of genes involved in type I interferon antiviral responses and IgG1 antibody synthesis (Fredrickson et al., 2013).
source: The CTRA is characterized by increased expression of genes involved in inflammation and decreased expression of genes involved in type I interferon antiviral responses and IgG1 antibody synthesis (Fredrickson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fredrickson et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies investigated a limited set of psychosocial experiences and did not resolve whether these pathways are causally linked to health outcomes or rather a consequence of disease status.
source: However, these studies investigated a limited set of psychosocial experiences and did not resolve whether these pathways are causally linked to health outcomes or rather a consequence of disease status.
evidence: This is a critique of previous studies that motivates the current study's approach.

claim: Several approaches have been developed for investigating the role of gene expression in complex trait variation (Nica et al., 2010; Marigorta et al., 2017; Võsa et al., 2018; Nica and Dermitzakis, 2008).
source: Several approaches have been developed for investigating the role of gene expression in complex trait variation (Nica et al., 2010; Marigorta et al., 2017; Võsa et al., 2018; Nica and Dermitzakis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Nica et al., 2010; Marigorta et al., 2017; Võsa et al., 2018; Nica and Dermitzakis, 2008.

claim: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) and other Mendelian randomization (MR) approaches have been used to integrate genetic effects on gene expression and on complex traits to establish causal links between a gene and a phenotype (Gusev et al., 2016).
source: Recently, transcriptome-wide association studies [TWAS] and other Mendelian randomization (MR) approaches have been used to integrate genetic effects on gene expression and on complex traits to establish causal links between a gene and a phenotype (Gusev et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gusev et al., 2016.

claim: MR approaches have been developed in epidemiology to examine the causal effect of a modifiable exposure on disease without conducting a randomized trial.
source: MR approaches have been developed in epidemiology to examine the causal effect of a modifiable exposure on disease without conducting a randomized trial.
evidence: This is a description of the MR approach based on established knowledge in epidemiology.

claim: MR designs use the genotype association with the two variables of interest to control for reverse causation and confounding.
source: MR designs use the genotype association with the two variables of interest to control for reverse causation and confounding.
evidence: This is a description of how MR designs work, based on established knowledge.

claim: Very few studies of genetic regulation of gene expression (eQTL mapping) in humans have included comprehensive information on psychosocial exposures.
source: Very few studies of genetic regulation of gene expression (expression quantitative trait loci, eQTL mapping) in humans have included comprehensive information on psychosocial exposures, and no study to date has been able to determine the likelihood of a causal relationship between psychosocial experiences, gene expression, and asthma.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: No study to date has been able to determine the likelihood of a causal relationship between psychosocial experiences, gene expression, and asthma.
source: Very few studies of genetic regulation of gene expression (expression quantitative trait loci, eQTL mapping) in humans have included comprehensive information on psychosocial exposures, and no study to date has been able to determine the likelihood of a causal relationship between psychosocial experiences, gene expression, and asthma.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The study aims at filling the gap by combining genetic and well-characterized psychosocial data from a cohort of children with asthma living in Metro Detroit.
source: This study aims at filling this gap by combining genetic and well-characterized psychosocial data from a cohort of children with asthma living in Metro Detroit (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's aim, supported by the study design shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The study identified significant transcriptional signatures for 31 out of 53 variables.
source: We identified significant transcriptional signatures for 31 out of 53 variables (Figure 1b–e, Figure 1—source data 1, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a specific finding reported in the results section and shown in Figure 1b-e.

claim: An independent longitudinal dataset was used to validate the transcriptional signatures.
source: We used an independent longitudinal dataset to validate the transcriptional signatures.
evidence: This is a description of the validation approach used in the study.

claim: Significant correlations were found in the observed and imputed changes for the majority of variables (Spearman's correlation p-value<0.05).
source: We found significant correlations in the observed and imputed changes for the majority of variables (Spearman's correlation p-value<0.05; e.g., Figure 1f, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the validation analysis, shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Transcriptional signatures of the SES measures showed a strong overlap with each other.
source: Transcriptional signatures of the SES measures showed a strong overlap with each other (Figure 2), suggesting that they may have very similar molecular effects or measure the same factors.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Subjective SES was significantly correlated with objective maternal responsiveness (r = −0.3, p=1.1 * 10−6).
source: For example, subjective SES was significantly correlated with objective maternal responsiveness, family conflict, and self-reported self-disclosure, which is the extent to which the youths talk about their thoughts and feelings (r = −0.3, p=1.1 * 10−6, r = 0.29, p=4.26 * 10−6, r = 0.66, p=3 * 10−32, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Subjective SES was significantly correlated with family conflict (r = 0.29, p=4.26 * 10−6).
source: For example, subjective SES was significantly correlated with objective maternal responsiveness, family conflict, and self-reported self-disclosure, which is the extent to which the youths talk about their thoughts and feelings (r = −0.3, p=1.1 * 10−6, r = 0.29, p=4.26 * 10−6, r = 0.66, p=3 * 10−32, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Subjective SES was significantly correlated with self-reported self-disclosure (r = 0.66, p=3 * 10−32).
source: For example, subjective SES was significantly correlated with objective maternal responsiveness, family conflict, and self-reported self-disclosure, which is the extent to which the youths talk about their thoughts and feelings (r = −0.3, p=1.1 * 10−6, r = 0.29, p=4.26 * 10−6, r = 0.66, p=3 * 10−32, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Correlations between transcriptional signatures reflect correlations between measured variables.
source: Overall, correlations between transcriptional signatures reflect correlations between measured variables (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), yet they are stronger between the transcriptional signatures, highlighting the denoising effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Correlations are stronger between the transcriptional signatures than between measured variables, highlighting the denoising effect.
source: Overall, correlations between transcriptional signatures reflect correlations between measured variables (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), yet they are stronger between the transcriptional signatures, highlighting the denoising effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Perceived responsiveness was associated with changes in gene expression for 143 genes.
source: For example, perceived responsiveness and self-disclosure were associated with changes in gene expression for 143 and 3279 genes, respectively (Supplementary file 1e, f).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Self-disclosure was associated with changes in gene expression for 3279 genes.
source: For example, perceived responsiveness and self-disclosure were associated with changes in gene expression for 143 and 3279 genes, respectively (Supplementary file 1e, f).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes positively associated with perceived responsiveness were enriched for biological processes relative to the response to IL18.
source: Genes positively associated with perceived responsiveness were enriched for biological processes relative to the response to IL18, while genes positively associated with self-disclosure were enriched for the interferon 1 pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes positively associated with self-disclosure were enriched for the interferon 1 pathway.
source: Genes positively associated with perceived responsiveness were enriched for biological processes relative to the response to IL18, while genes positively associated with self-disclosure were enriched for the interferon 1 pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Transcriptional signatures of asthma severity correlated with those for psychosocial variables, specifically with SES and social relationships, but not emotionality.
source: When we correlated transcriptional signatures of asthma severity with those for psychosocial variables, we observed overlap with SES and social relationships, but not emotionality.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis between asthma severity and psychosocial variables.

claim: Significant positive correlations were found between the transcriptional signatures of lung function (percent-predicted FEV1) and psychosocial measures of self-disclosure (r = 0.42, p=4.9 * 10−12).
source: In particular, we found significant positive correlations between the transcriptional signatures of lung function (percent-predicted FEV1) and psychosocial measures of self-disclosure (r = 0.42, p=4.9 * 10−12) and subjective SES (r = 0.36, p=3.3 * 10−9).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Significant positive correlations were found between the transcriptional signatures of lung function (percent-predicted FEV1) and subjective SES (r = 0.36, p=3.3 * 10−9).
source: In particular, we found significant positive correlations between the transcriptional signatures of lung function (percent-predicted FEV1) and psychosocial measures of self-disclosure (r = 0.42, p=4.9 * 10−12) and subjective SES (r = 0.36, p=3.3 * 10−9).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Objective maternal responsiveness was negatively correlated with lung function (r = −0.19, p=0.002).
source: Unexpectedly, objective maternal responsiveness was negatively correlated with lung function (r = −0.19, p=0.002), and percent unoccupied properties in the neighborhood (r = 0.41, p=7.8 * 10−12) was positively correlated with lung function.
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: Percent unoccupied properties in the neighborhood was positively correlated with lung function (r = 0.41, p=7.8 * 10−12).
source: Unexpectedly, objective maternal responsiveness was negatively correlated with lung function (r = −0.19, p=0.002), and percent unoccupied properties in the neighborhood (r = 0.41, p=7.8 * 10−12) was positively correlated with lung function.
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: The transcriptional signature of self-disclosure was significantly associated with nightly asthma symptoms (r = 0.27, p=1.2 * 10−5).
source: We also found that the transcriptional signature of self-disclosure was also significantly associated with other measures of asthma, such as nightly asthma symptoms (r = 0.27, p=1.2 * 10−5) and asthma severity (r = −0.32, p=2.9 * 10−7), echoing the large body of work on the importance of self-disclosure for health (Pennebaker, 1995).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: The transcriptional signature of self-disclosure was significantly associated with asthma severity (r = −0.32, p=2.9 * 10−7).
source: We also found that the transcriptional signature of self-disclosure was also significantly associated with other measures of asthma, such as nightly asthma symptoms (r = 0.27, p=1.2 * 10−5) and asthma severity (r = −0.32, p=2.9 * 10−7), echoing the large body of work on the importance of self-disclosure for health (Pennebaker, 1995).
evidence: This is a specific correlation finding reported in the results section.

claim: There is a large body of work on the importance of self-disclosure for health (Pennebaker, 1995).
source: We also found that the transcriptional signature of self-disclosure was also significantly associated with other measures of asthma, such as nightly asthma symptoms (r = 0.27, p=1.2 * 10−5) and asthma severity (r = −0.32, p=2.9 * 10−7), echoing the large body of work on the importance of self-disclosure for health (Pennebaker, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pennebaker, 1995.

claim: The results provide a potential mechanism through gene expression changes in leukocytes for previously reported links between SES and asthma symptoms (Litonjua et al., 1999; Mielck et al., 1996).
source: These results provide a potential mechanism through gene expression changes in leukocytes for previously reported links between SES and asthma symptoms (Litonjua et al., 1999; Mielck et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous research, supported by citations to Litonjua et al., 1999; Mielck et al., 1996.

claim: Past research has found emotionality to be a strong predictor of asthma severity (Lehrer et al., 1993).
source: Past research has also found emotionality to be a strong predictor of asthma severity (Lehrer et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lehrer et al., 1993.

claim: The transcriptional signatures of blood composition were associated with asthma symptoms, with a positive correlation for proportion of lymphocytes and negative correlation for proportion of neutrophils.
source: Notably, the transcriptional signatures of blood composition were also associated with asthma symptoms, with a positive correlation for proportion of lymphocytes and negative correlation for proportion of neutrophils (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several blood cell types play an important role in asthma severity and exacerbations (Mamessier et al., 2008; Vedel-Krogh et al., 2017; Bigler et al., 2017; Ray and Kolls, 2017; Lima-Matos et al., 2018; Casciano et al., 2016; Sinz et al., 2017).
source: Given the important role of several blood cell types in asthma severity and exacerbations (Mamessier et al., 2008; Vedel-Krogh et al., 2017; Bigler et al., 2017; Ray and Kolls, 2017; Lima-Matos et al., 2018; Casciano et al., 2016; Sinz et al., 2017), it is possible that transcriptional changes associated with blood composition mediated the correlations between psychosocial experiences and asthma outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Mamessier et al., 2008; Vedel-Krogh et al., 2017; Bigler et al., 2017; Ray and Kolls, 2017; Lima-Matos et al., 2018; Casciano et al., 2016; Sinz et al., 2017.

claim: It is possible that transcriptional changes associated with blood composition mediated the correlations between psychosocial experiences and asthma outcomes.
source: Given the important role of several blood cell types in asthma severity and exacerbations (Mamessier et al., 2008; Vedel-Krogh et al., 2017; Bigler et al., 2017; Ray and Kolls, 2017; Lima-Matos et al., 2018; Casciano et al., 2016; Sinz et al., 2017), it is possible that transcriptional changes associated with blood composition mediated the correlations between psychosocial experiences and asthma outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism underlying the observed correlations.

claim: The study performed cis-eQTL mapping and identified 8610 genes with at least one eQTL (eGenes, 10% false discovery rate [FDR]).
source: To examine local genetic effects on leukocyte gene expression, we performed cis-eQTL mapping and identified 8610 genes with at least one eQTL (eGenes, 10% false discovery rate [FDR], Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: The eGenes were enriched in Genotype-Tissue Expression Project (GTEx) whole blood eGenes (Aguet et al., 2020) (Fisher's test OR = 3.2, p-value<2.2 * 10−16).
source: These eGenes were enriched in Genotype-Tissue Expression Project (GTEx) whole blood eGenes (Aguet et al., 2020) (Fisher's test OR = 3.2, p-value<2.2 * 10−16), but we also identified additional 1801 eGenes that were not detected by GTEx in whole blood.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis comparing the study's eGenes to GTEx eGenes.

claim: The study identified additional 1801 eGenes that were not detected by GTEx in whole blood.
source: These eGenes were enriched in Genotype-Tissue Expression Project (GTEx) whole blood eGenes (Aguet et al., 2020) (Fisher's test OR = 3.2, p-value<2.2 * 10−16), but we also identified additional 1801 eGenes that were not detected by GTEx in whole blood.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of the study's eGenes to GTEx eGenes.

claim: The study used the method for probabilistic TWAS analysis (PTWAS) (Zhang et al., 2020).
source: We used the method for probabilistic TWAS analysis (PTWAS) (Zhang et al., 2020), which improves upon previous TWAS methods by ensuring only strong IVs are used, and is designed to allow for validating the causality assumption (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the method used in the study, supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: PTWAS improves upon previous TWAS methods by ensuring only strong IVs are used, and is designed to allow for validating the causality assumption.
source: We used the method for probabilistic TWAS analysis (PTWAS) (Zhang et al., 2020), which improves upon previous TWAS methods by ensuring only strong IVs are used, and is designed to allow for validating the causality assumption (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of PTWAS over previous TWAS methods.

claim: The study identified 2806 eGenes in the GTEx dataset that were causally associated with asthma and allergic diseases (hay fever, eczema, and allergic rhinitis) (5% FDR).
source: We identified 2806 eGenes in the GTEx dataset that were causally associated with asthma and allergic diseases (hay fever, eczema, and allergic rhinitis) (5% FDR).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the PTWAS analysis.

claim: Of the 2806 eGenes causally associated with asthma and allergic diseases, 853 were eGenes in the study's dataset.
source: Of these, 853 were eGenes in our dataset (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the overlap analysis between PTWAS results and the study's eGenes.

claim: The study discovered 344 significant interaction eQTLs across 134 unique genes (10% FDR).
source: We discovered 344 significant interaction eQTLs across 134 unique genes (10% FDR; Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the GxE eQTL mapping analysis, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Interaction eQTLs were found for all four blood composition signatures (proportion of lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils with 81, 65, 27, and 25 GxE interactions, respectively).
source: We found interaction eQTLs for all four blood composition signatures (proportion of lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils with 81, 65, 27, and 25 GxE interactions, respectively), which represent cell-type-specific eQTLs (57.6% of all GxE eQTLs).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the GxE eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: Blood composition signatures represent cell-type-specific eQTLs (57.6% of all GxE eQTLs).
source: We found interaction eQTLs for all four blood composition signatures (proportion of lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils with 81, 65, 27, and 25 GxE interactions, respectively), which represent cell-type-specific eQTLs (57.6% of all GxE eQTLs).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GxE eQTL findings for blood composition.

claim: 101 of the 108 blood-interacting eGenes (93.5%) were also identified as genes with interaction eQTLs with cell-type composition in GTEx whole blood (Kim-Hellmuth et al., 2020).
source: 101 of the 108 blood-interacting eGenes (93.5%) were also identified as genes with interaction eQTLs with cell-type composition in GTEx whole blood (Kim-Hellmuth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of the study's GxE eGenes to GTEx GxE eGenes, supported by a citation to Kim-Hellmuth et al., 2020.

claim: The study identified 124 GxE interaction effects on gene expression with psychosocial experiences across 77 genes, including self-disclosure (48 genes), subjective SES (40 genes), and objective maternal responsiveness (16 genes).
source: We identified 124 GxE interaction effects on gene expression with psychosocial experiences across 77 genes, including self-disclosure (48 genes), subjective SES (40 genes), and objective maternal responsiveness (16 genes) (Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the GxE eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: GxE effects for psychosocial experiences only partially overlapped (77%) with GxE effects observed for blood composition.
source: These only partially overlapped (77%) GxE effects observed for blood composition and included interactions specific to psychosocial factors (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of GxE effects for psychosocial experiences and blood composition, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: After correcting for blood cell composition, the study observed 125 significant GxE effects (10% FDR).
source: To evaluate whether the interactions with psychosocial experiences may be mediated by cell composition, we repeated the GxE mapping after correcting for blood cell composition. We observed 125 significant GxE effects (10% FDR) after removing the effect of blood composition differences (Figure 3—source data 6).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the GxE eQTL mapping analysis after correcting for blood cell composition.

claim: The GxE eQTLs detected with the measured variables were significantly enriched for low p-values in the GxE eQTLs detected with the transcriptional signatures.
source: We found that the GxE eQTLs detected with the measured variables (Figure 3—source data 7) were significantly enriched for low p-values in the GxE eQTLs detected with the transcriptional signatures (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the interaction effects were highly significantly correlated (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis comparing GxE eQTLs detected with measured variables and transcriptional signatures, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction effects between GxE eQTLs detected with measured variables and transcriptional signatures were highly significantly correlated.
source: We found that the GxE eQTLs detected with the measured variables (Figure 3—source data 7) were significantly enriched for low p-values in the GxE eQTLs detected with the transcriptional signatures (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the interaction effects were highly significantly correlated (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis comparing GxE eQTLs detected with measured variables and transcriptional signatures.

claim: 94.8% of the study's GxE genes replicated in other datasets of GxE in gene expression (p<0.05).
source: We found that 94.8% of our GxE genes replicated in other datasets of GxE in gene expression (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the replication analysis comparing the study's GxE genes to other published GxE datasets.

claim: 62 interaction eGenes for psychosocial experiences overlapped with interaction eGenes in response to pathogens (Lee et al., 2014; Barreiro et al., 2012; Çalışkan et al., 2015; Nédélec et al., 2016).
